newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: JSE RISE UNLIKELY TO TEMPT FOREIGNERS TO S.AFRICA.
newsitem.headline: JSE RISE UNLIKELY TO TEMPT FOREIGNERS TO S.AFRICA.

text.p: South African shares have gone from strength to strength recently, but analysts said on Wednesday their advances were unlikely to woo foreign investors still keeping a wary eye on the country's economic fundamentals.
Dealers have hiked up prices as stocks in New York, London and other major financial markets have set new records.
The Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) has not missed out on the party and on Tuesday the all-share index ended at a record closing high of 7,073.1, hitting an all-time intra-day high of 7,099.4.
But analysts said foreign investors, while impressed by the market's growth, were still watchful of a weak currency and a weak balance of payments position.

"Funds are still looking at the level of foreign exchange reserves, which indicate the balance of payments deficit. What the market is doing will be sidelined by the balance of payments," said Johann Els, economist at life assurer Old Mutual.
Latest Reserve bank figures show combined gold and foreign exchange reserves fell 35.68 million rand in September to 10.04 billion rand, equivalent to just four weeks import cover.

Analysts noted the poor balance of payments was keeping interest rates high, which was bad news for corporate earnings. The Bank rate currently stands at 16 percent with the prime rate at 19.25 percent.

The weakness of the rand was also putting a dampener on foreign interest, with many international funds sticking to strong currencies in the face of a buoyant Wall Street and seeing no reason to gamble on the JSE and its rocky rand.
Since mid-February the rand has lost a quarter of its value against the dollar, easily wiping out the 3.6 percent advance in the all-share index since then.
Many analysts believe the currency is likely to depreciate further, with ABN AMRO on Wednesday predicting a fall to 4.60 by the end of this year.
Meanwhile, the JSE has shown signs that its rise may be short-lived, with the all-share index closing on Wednesday down 0.71 percent at 7,022.9.

"It has not been a very convincing breakthrough, even in rand terms. We got to around these levels earlier this year and the JSE didn't build on them like the Dow did," said Denzil Newman, portfolio manager at Syfrets Asset Management.
"I doubt that the rise will, by itself, attract many more people in to the JSE," he added.
Analysts said foreign investors were split into two camps on whether to invest in South African shares.
On the positive side recent international share issues from such established blue-chip South African firms as AECI Ltd and South African Breweries Ltd have been well-received.
But on the other hand some investors, wary of the weak rand and violent crime, are withdrawing. "Some fund managers have wanted to get their lines completely out," said one portfolio manager.
The mix of opinion, both domestically and abroad, seems to be reflected in the JSE's gains being unsteady, analysts said.
"It is a well-balanced market with neither the bulls nor the bears dominating and that seems to be reflected in the views of foreigners too," Newman said.
Analysts said the p/e (price earnings ratio) of the industrial and all share index would have to dip below 15 before foreigners were tempted to the JSE in large numbers.
This had briefly occurred earlier this year, but as the p/e ticked up to 15 again, foreigners had bailed out.
"The p/e is likely to stay above 15 for both markets for most of the next 12 months," Newman said.
Until the p/e improves foreigners are likely to cherry pick their stocks where growth looks strong.
"There are emerging market opportunities here. They (foreign investors) are prepared to take the view that some of these companies are growth firms," said one analyst.
